🧀 Crispy Parmesan Chicken with Garlic Potatoes & Green Beans 🍗🥔 This Crispy Parmesan Chicken with Garlic Potatoes & Green Beans is an easy sheet-pan dinner packed with bold flavor. Juicy oven-roasted chicken is coated in a crispy Parmesan crust, while buttery garlic potatoes and tender green beans roast alongside for a complete, satisfying family meal with minimal cleanup. Ingredients For the Chicken • 4 boneless, skinless chicken breasts • 2 tbsp olive oil • ¾ cup grated Parmesan cheese • ½ cup panko breadcrumbs • 1 tsp garlic powder • 1 tsp Italian seasoning • ½ tsp smoked paprika • ¾ tsp salt • ½ tsp black pepper For the Potatoes • 1½ lbs baby Yukon Gold potatoes, halved • 1 tbsp olive oil • 2 tbsp melted butter • 1 tsp garlic powder • ½ tsp paprika • Salt and black pepper, to taste For the Green Beans • 12 oz fresh green beans, trimmed • 1 tbsp olive oil • 2 garlic cloves, minced • 1 tbsp melted butter • Salt and black pepper, to taste For Garnish • 2 tbsp chopped fresh parsley • Lemon wedges Instructions 1. Preheat the oven to 425°F (220°C). Lightly grease a large sheet pan or line it with parchment paper. 2. Toss the potatoes with olive oil, melted butter, garlic powder, paprika, salt, and pepper. Spread them evenly on one side of the pan and roast for 15 minutes. 3. In a shallow bowl, combine the Parmesan cheese, panko breadcrumbs, garlic powder, Italian seasoning, smoked paprika, salt, and black pepper. 4. Brush both sides of the chicken breasts with olive oil, then press them firmly into the Parmesan mixture until well coated. 5. Remove the sheet pan from the oven and move the potatoes to one side. Arrange the coated chicken in the center. 6. Toss the green beans with olive oil, melted butter, minced garlic, salt, and pepper, then place them beside the chicken. 7. Bake for 20–25 minutes, or until the chicken reaches an internal temperature of 165°F (74°C) and the potatoes are fork-tender. 8. Switch the oven to broil and cook for 2–3 minutes until the Parmesan crust is extra crispy and golden. 9. Sprinkle with fresh parsley and serve with lemon wedges. Serving Suggestions Serve with Caesar salad, garlic bread, roasted carrots, steamed broccoli, or creamy ranch dipping sauce for a complete restaurant-style dinner. Storage Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 4 days. Reheat in the oven or air fryer to keep the chicken crispy. Prep Time: 15 minutes Cook Time: 40 minutes Total Time: 55 minutes Servings: 4 Calories: Approximately 610 per serving #ParmesanChicken #SheetPanDinner #EasyDinner #ComfortFood #FamilyMeals

Le couvre-chef masculin n’est jamais un simple accessoire. Il structure une silhouette, signe une époque, révèle une intention. La gavroche (Newsboy / Baker boy cap) Plus ample, composée de plusieurs pans, elle offre du relief et une présence marquée. D’inspiration populaire au départ, elle est aujourd’hui un marqueur de caractère et de style assumé. Le béret (Beret) Intemporel, circulaire, sans visière. Il incarne une élégance intellectuelle et continentale. Porté avec justesse, il traverse les classes sociales et les décennies sans jamais disparaître. Le fedora Calotte pincée, bord moyen à large, souvent en feutre. C’est le chapeau de la ville par excellence, associé au costume, au manteau long, à une allure structurée. Il suggère autorité et distinction. Le trilby Plus court et plus nerveux que le fedora. Bord réduit, esprit plus moderne. Il convient aux silhouettes urbaines et aux tenues plus légères. Le homburg Formel, reconnaissable à son bord ourlé et sa calotte marquée. Longtemps associé aux hommes d’influence, il conserve une gravité assumée. Le pork pie Calotte basse et plate, allure compacte. Popularisé par le jazz et certaines contre-cultures, il demande une vraie maîtrise stylistique. Le gambler Bord plat, calotte légèrement creusée. Inspiré du western raffiné, il impose une présence forte et une silhouette affirmée. Le panama Chapeau de paille tressée, clair, respirant. Indissociable de l’été élégant. Il protège sans alourdir, suggérant voyage et nonchalance maîtrisée. En définitive, le couvre-chef n’est ni décoratif ni anodin. Il est une signature. Cozy & Affordable Baked Chicken Dinner 🍗🤎 Tonight I was going for cozy, comforting, and affordable, and this is one of my go-to dinners when I want something simple but still really good. Ingredients: * Chicken legs * Olive oil * Garlic powder * Onion powder * Paprika * Seasoning salt * Black pepper * Italian seasoning * 1 orange bell pepper, sliced * 1 green bell pepper, sliced * 1 onion, sliced * 2 cans cream of mushroom soup * ½–1 cup chicken broth * Jasmine rice * French-style green beans * Buttermilk biscuits * Honey for glazing Instructions: 1. Season the chicken legs with garlic powder, onion powder, paprika, seasoning salt, black pepper, and Italian seasoning. 2. Drizzle with olive oil and mix well so the seasoning coats the chicken. 3. Slice the peppers and onion. 4. Sauté the peppers and onions in a skillet until they begin to soften. 5. Add the cream of mushroom soup and chicken broth. Stir until smooth and creamy. 6. Place the seasoned chicken in a baking dish and pour the creamy mixture over the top. 7. Bake at 375°F for about 50–60 minutes, or until the chicken reaches 165°F internally and is fully cooked. 8. Serve with jasmine rice, French-style green beans, and a warm buttermilk biscuit finished with a little honey. Affordable, filling, and the perfect comfort dinner. ✨ CARAMELIZED BAKED CHICKEN THIGHS ✨ 🍗🍯🧄🔥😍 These caramelized baked chicken thighs are sticky, sweet, and fall-apart tender. Smothered in a rich, glossy glaze that bakes right into the meat, this simple recipe delivers incredible flavor with minimal effort! 🍴 Ingredients: - 8 chicken thighs (bone-in or boneless) - ⅓ cup honey (or maple syrup) - ¼ cup low-sodium soy sauce - 2 tbsp brown sugar, packed - 4 cloves garlic, minced - 1 tbsp olive oil - 1 tbsp apple cider vinegar (or fresh lemon juice) - 1 tsp onion powder - 1 tsp smoked paprika - 1 tsp salt - ½ tsp black pepper 👩🏽‍🍳 Instructions: 1. Preheat your oven to 400°F (200°C). Lightly grease a 9x13-inch glass baking dish. 2. Pat the chicken thighs completely dry with paper towels. Season both sides with salt, black pepper, onion powder, and smoked paprika. 3. In a small bowl, whisk together the honey, soy sauce, brown sugar, minced garlic, olive oil, and apple cider vinegar until smooth and well combined. 4. Arrange the seasoned chicken thighs skin-side up in a single layer in the baking dish. 5. Pour the glaze evenly over the chicken, making sure each piece is thoroughly coated. 6. Bake uncovered for 35–40 minutes (for bone-in thighs) or 25–30 minutes (for boneless), basting the chicken with the pan sauce halfway through cooking. 7. Turn the broiler on for the final 2–3 minutes to get that rich, bubbly, caramelized glaze on top (watch closely so it doesn't burn!). 8. Let the chicken rest for 5 minutes, then spoon the remaining pan juices generously over the top before serving! 📝 Notes: Using bone-in, skin-on chicken thighs keeps the meat exceptionally juicy and gives you the best rich flavor, but boneless skinless thighs work fantastically well too—just reduce the baking time by about 10 minutes. ⏱️ Prep Time: 10 minutes 🍳 Cook Time: 40 minutes ⏰ Total Time: 50 minutes #BakedChickenThighs #CaramelizedChicken #HoneyGarlicChicken #EasyDinner #ChickenRecipes

pricing my work is truly my LEAST favourite thing 😭  especially after trying to look closer at the numbers behind my small ceramic business. i’m trying to map out the potential 1, 3, and 5 year revenue and expense projections to see if investing in a kiln and building this business actually makes any sense. at my current $30-$65 price point, i’m losing money selling my work and cannot justify a kiln. i’ve made the terrifying decision to raise my prices by 25-30%. the money will go towards expanding production (investing. in a kiln & shelving), upgrading my website, expanding to ship to the US, and finally, offering private lessons and workshops.  with the price increase, I will still need to survive 6 months - 1 year without a livable wage / making profit. i’ll be focusing on my higher-margin petal bowls and bring in some more affordable $25 products like spoon rests and trinket dishes to keep things as accessible as possible. my mugs are not viable as they take me 2hrs each, but i’m going to keep making them for now and hope i can speed it up. no more lidded jars outside of speciality collections as the margins are too low.  i’m also going to try to secure 1-2 freelance social media clients to provide me with some supplement income as a buffer. this is the behind the scenes of small ceramics business’ that you normally don’t see, because it’s not nearly as cute or fun as the pots themselves. #potterybusiness #ceramics #smallbusiness #priceincrease #handmadeceramics

One-Pan Chicken with Buttered Noodles This One-Pan Chicken with Buttered Noodles is cozy, creamy, and full of flavor. Golden seared chicken sits over tender noodles tossed in a buttery garlic sauce, making it an easy family dinner with very little cleanup. Ingredients: 6 boneless, skinless chicken thighs or chicken breasts 12 ounces egg noodles 2 tablespoons olive oil 4 tablespoons butter, divided 3 cloves garlic, minced 1 teaspoon paprika 1 teaspoon garlic powder 1/2 teaspoon onion powder 1 teaspoon salt 1/2 teaspoon black pepper 2 cups chicken broth 1 cup heavy cream 1/2 cup grated parmesan cheese 1 tablespoon chopped parsley, optional Instructions: Season the chicken with paprika, garlic powder, onion powder, salt, and black pepper. Heat olive oil and 2 tablespoons butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add the chicken and cook for 5 to 6 minutes per side, until golden and cooked through. Remove chicken and set aside. Add garlic to the same skillet and cook for 30 seconds until fragrant. Pour in chicken broth and heavy cream, then stir well and bring to a gentle simmer. Add the egg noodles, cover, and cook for 8 to 10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the noodles are tender. Stir in parmesan cheese and remaining 2 tablespoons butter until creamy and smooth. Return the chicken to the skillet and spoon some sauce over the top. Cook for 2 to 3 minutes until heated through. Sprinkle with parsley if using and serve hot. Store leftovers in the fridge for up to 3 days. Prep Time: 10 minutes | Cook Time: 25 minutes | Total Time: 35 minutes Servings: 4 to 6 | Calories: 560 per serving

Teriyaki Chicken Veggie Rice Bake A delicious one-pan casserole loaded with juicy chicken, fluffy rice, crisp-tender vegetables, and a homemade teriyaki sauce. It's an easy, family-friendly dinner that's packed with flavor and perfect for busy weeknights. Ingredients Chicken & Rice Bake 1½ pounds boneless, skinless chicken breasts, cut into bite-sized pieces 3 cups cooked white rice 2 cups broccoli florets 1 cup diced carrots 1 red bell pepper, chopped ½ red onion, chopped ½ cup frozen peas 2 green onions, thinly sliced 1 tablespoon sesame seeds (optional) Homemade Teriyaki Sauce ½ cup low-sodium soy sauce ⅓ cup honey or brown sugar ¼ cup water 2 tablespoons rice vinegar 1 tablespoon sesame oil 3 garlic cloves, minced 1 teaspoon freshly grated ginger 1 tablespoon cornstarch 2 tablespoons water Instructions Preheat your oven to 375°F and lightly coat a 9x13-inch baking dish with cooking spray or a thin layer of oil. To prepare the teriyaki sauce, combine the soy sauce, honey, ¼ cup water, rice vinegar, sesame oil, garlic, and ginger in a small saucepan. Bring the mixture to a gentle simmer over medium heat and cook for about 2 to 3 minutes. In a separate small bowl, whisk together the cornstarch and 2 tablespoons of water until smooth. Stir the slurry into the simmering sauce and continue cooking for another 1 to 2 minutes, or until the sauce thickens. Remove from the heat. Heat a large skillet over medium heat. Add the chicken pieces and cook for 6 to 8 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the chicken is browned and fully cooked. Add the broccoli, carrots, bell pepper, red onion, and peas to the skillet. Cook for another 4 to 5 minutes, just until the vegetables begin to soften while still keeping a slight crunch. Stir the cooked rice into the skillet, then pour in half of the teriyaki sauce. Mix everything together until the rice, chicken, and vegetables are evenly coated. Transfer the mixture into the prepared baking dish and spread it into an even layer. Pour the remaining teriyaki sauce evenly over the top. Bake uncovered for 15 to 20 minutes, or until the casserole is thoroughly heated and bubbling around the edges. Remove from the oven and garnish with sliced green onions and sesame seeds before serving. Storage Store any leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Reheat in the microwave or oven until warmed through. Prep Time: 15 minutes Cook Time: 30 minutes Total Time: 45 minutes Servings: 6 Calories: Approximately 430 per serving

Ils vont essayer de comprendre… mais ils ne pourront pas reproduire. Parce que ce que tu vois, ce n’est pas un look. C’est une vision. J’ai pris l’ADN du cowboy et je l’ai projeté ailleurs. Chapeau crème oversized qui domine la silhouette, presque comme une ombre portée sur le futur. Denim retravaillé, brûlé, patiné, déconstruit… chaque trace donne l’impression qu’il a déjà vécu plusieurs époques. Les coutures visibles, les déchirures brutes, les transitions de textures — rien n’est propre, tout est intentionnel. Superposition instable mais maîtrisée : une veste tailoring texturée qui casse les codes, une autre en denim posée sur l’épaule comme une armure incomplète. Un gilet structuré beige qui recentre le chaos et impose une ligne. Une chemise en dessous, presque classique, pour rappeler que le contrôle existe encore dans la rupture. Et ces bottes lourdes, ancrées, solides… pendant que le reste du corps échappe aux règles. La pose n’est pas une pose. C’est un moment suspendu. Un déséquilibre contrôlé, un corps qui penche mais ne tombe pas, un geste figé entre passé et futur. Le décor classique derrière moi représente ce qui existe déjà. Moi, je représente ce qui arrive. Je ne porte pas des vêtements. Je construis une identité visuelle. Le style ne m’a jamais créé. C’est moi qui crée le style. Tu peux acheter les pièces. Mais tu ne pourras jamais acheter la vision. Les marques cherchent des images. Les artistes cherchent une direction. Moi, je crée les deux. Si tu vois plus loin que le vêtement, on peut construire quelque chose. Sinon… regarde encore.

In my YouTube video this weekend I’m recreating some pots I haven’t thrown since 2014, specially store jars with inset, internal galleries and thin lids with thrown knobs. You can find a link to the fully narrated video via the Linktree in my profile’s biography.   I’ve lied a little bit. I did create jars that were similar to this during my apprenticeship with Lisa Hammond between 2014-2017, yet they were bellied pieces with a gallery closer to the jars I make these days, yet they unusual thrown knobs that were in themselves similar to small bowls.   To create pots with internal galleries like this you need to split the rim. One section becomes the lip, the other is coaxed inside and carefully set horizontal to essentially become a ledge onto which the lid can be held aloft. This alone is a tricky task and it involves throwing a form with enough material in the lip to withstand such a manoeuvre. Secondly, there’s the small disc-like lid, a form that’s thrown off-the-hump and then the following day it’s trimmed back to have its more exacting shape and the knob is thrown on, again, a tricky task as it involves fiddly, fingertip throwing and a lot of accuracy.   All of this and more will be covered in my longer, narrated YouTube upload. I enjoyed making these and since it has been such a long time since I’ve crafted them, my skillset in the interim has improved massively, thus I could apply newly learnt techniques and ability into making shapes I used to struggle with to some degree. I hope you like the film if you happen to click over and watch it, it’s greatly appreciated if you do as it helps to keep the lights on in the workshop.   #pottery #ceramics #handmade #jar #satisfying

Making money from a digital product isn’t about getting lucky. It’s about having a simple system and executing it consistently. Here’s the step-by-step 👇 1️⃣ Pick ONE problem Think about something your audience is struggling with. Weight loss. Confidence. Canva. Meditation. Making money. Content creation. Find a problem → create a solution. 2️⃣ Turn your knowledge into a simple product 📕💡 You don’t need to create a 200-page masterpiece. Create something that helps someone go from A → B. A guide, checklist, template, ebook or resource can be enough if it actually solves the problem. 3️⃣ Create content around the problem 📱 Don’t just post “buy my ebook.” Teach. Share tips. Show mistakes. Break down strategies. Tell stories. Answer common questions. Give people a reason to trust you BEFORE you ask them to buy. 4️⃣ Add a simple CTA 🔗 Tell people exactly what to do next. “Comment GUIDE.” “Link in bio.” “DM me PDF.” Don’t make people guess how to get your product. 5️⃣ Make the offer clear 💰 Explain: What they get Who it’s for What problem it solves What they’ll learn Why it’s useful Clarity converts. 6️⃣ Repeat the process 🔄 One post might flop. That doesn’t mean the business doesn’t work. Keep creating. Keep testing hooks. Keep improving your offer. Keep listening to your audience. The goal isn’t to go viral once. The goal is to build a system that can keep generating attention and sales. So while someone is sitting there hating… You could be learning a skill, building an audience and creating another income stream. 🧠📈 Focus on building, not proving. Your results will always speak louder than their opinions. 🚀 Follow me for more practical ways to build and monetize your personal brand. 💰

How to create AI employees — start to finish, everything included The complete build of an AI employee, start to finish — the whole path in under four minutes. The agent underneath — every AI employee starts as an agent: a brain (the AI model), tools (real connections into your email, calendar, spreadsheets so it acts instead of only talking), and a loop (it works the job, checks itself, and keeps going until it's done). Feed the brain context and it works on YOUR business. The four upgrades that make it an employee — memory (corrections get written down and read back before every job — explain a thing once and it stays explained), permanent context (your world lives with it and changes as your business changes), skills (your way of doing a job, taught once, followed every time), and a schedule (an agent runs when you call it — an employee clocks in on its own, seven in the morning, inbox already sorted). The build tool — an AI coding assistant: Claude Code or Codex. That class of tool IS the agent machinery — it navigates your context, picks its next move, loops until the job is done, and carries memory between runs. You set it up in plain English, and when a piece you need exists nowhere, it writes that piece itself. The full assembly — pick one job, give it context, wire the tools, teach the skill, add memory, set the schedule. One rule built in: high-stakes moves wait for your yes; everything else runs around the clock. The ceiling — one employee becomes a pattern, patterns become a team, and the team becomes a department passing work to each other. This video is the skeleton of my entire curriculum — every step is a full course, taught from zero, step by step, about four months front to back.
